heading: Initialization controls training speed and trainable depth
definition: initializations matched to the activation function that keep signals and gradients from vanishing or exploding across layers let plain networks learn faster and train at greater depth (Glorot & Bengio 2010; He et al. 2015; Schoenholz et al. 2017). In very deep tanh networks, orthogonal weights learn faster than Gaussian weights of the same variance, and orthogonal convolution kernels let plain convolutional networks train at 10,000 layers (Pennington et al. 2017; Xiao et al. 2018).
summary: Several independent groups reproduce the findings that initialization affects whether training succeeds and that, under some conditions, orthogonal weights train deep tanh networks faster than Gaussian weights. Orthogonal and Gaussian training dynamics become nearly equal in wide networks at small learning rates in the neural tangent kernel regime, where a linear approximation around the initial parameters describes training; the 10,000-layer CNN demonstration remains an original-study result.

suggested_status.by_scale: R2 for the initialization-sensitive optimization findings at unclassified parameter size. counts: versions.V4.studies_by_size contains only 'not stated', so no reproducibility level can be assigned separately to the catalog's toy, <1B, 1–10B, 10–100B or >100B buckets. The exact Delta-Orthogonal 10,000-layer CNN result remains an original-source result.
suggested_status.reason: Nonoriginal reviewed deep-tanh comparisons reproduce the conditional orthogonal speed advantage in arXiv:2004.05867#R1, arXiv:2004.05867#R7, arXiv:2310.07765#R11, arXiv:2310.07765#R13 and arXiv:2310.07765#R15; arXiv:2202.02981#R7 extends initialization-dependent trainability to structured narrow ReLU networks. The checker assigns arXiv:2004.05867 to T5: its theoretical argument and NTK experiments qualify the speed advantage through nearly equal dynamics in wide, small-learning-rate NTK settings, while suitable deep tanh comparisons outside that regime retain it. The shallow equality in arXiv:2310.07765#R9 and arXiv:2310.07765#R10 is outside V4's very-deep comparison and supplies neither support nor a scope limit for that prediction. Supplied pre-check counts are versions.V4.verdicts.supports.studies=76, versions.V4.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original=7, versions.V4.verdicts.limits_scope.studies=31 and versions.V4.verdicts.challenges.studies=0; these are not checker-adjusted totals. The exact 10,000-layer kernel demonstration is still arXiv:1806.05393#R2.
suggested_status.open_questions: Independent reproduction of the exact Delta-Orthogonal 10,000-layer CNN experiment would strengthen that clause. Matched finite-width comparisons controlling learning rate, budget, first-layer updates and propagation statistics would clarify the mechanism. Initialization-only language-model depth sweeps and explicit parameter counts would establish scale-specific coverage.

source.title: Dynamical Isometry and a Mean Field Theory of CNNs: How to Train 10, 000-Layer Vanilla Convolutional Neural Networks
source.authors: Lechao Xiao; Yasaman Bahri; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein; S. Schoenholz; Jeffrey Pennington

original_result.setup: Xiao et al. compared orthogonal and equal-variance Gaussian initialization and tested Delta-Orthogonal CNNs on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
original_result.result: A 4,000-layer orthogonally initialized CNN reached 95% accuracy on MNIST after 10,000 steps, while Gaussian initialization stayed below 60% training and test accuracy after 90,000 steps. The study also reported training and test curves for Delta-Orthogonal CNNs up to 10,000 layers, without numerical training accuracy in the text.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

untested.what: Independent reproduction of the exact 10,000-layer plain CNN result using Delta-Orthogonal convolution kernels, including extension beyond its original tanh MNIST/CIFAR-10 settings.
untested.basis: arXiv:1806.05393#R2 is the original experiment. The supplied untested-parts lines retain this specific gap; arXiv:2202.02981#R7 uses a different structured initialization and binary MNIST, and arXiv:2406.01755 concerns sparse 1,000-layer networks. counts: versions.V4.original_sources_linked includes arXiv:1806.05393, while versions.V4.coverage_by_operation.scaling does not resolve initialization type or exact depth.

untested.what: A matched-variance Gaussian-versus-orthogonal learning-speed comparison in the very deep tanh SVHN setting.
untested.basis: The checker confirms that arXiv:1810.03785, Section 4.2, evaluates 200-layer, width-400 tanh networks on CIFAR-10 and SVHN using two critical orthogonal initializations and Euclidean, Stiefel and Oblique optimization, without a matched-variance Gaussian-versus-orthogonal learning-speed experiment. This gap is inferred from the experiments, not explicitly identified by the paper; no result rows are retained for this study. The later comparisons supplied here use MNIST or CIFAR-10 (arXiv:2004.05867#R1, arXiv:2310.07765#R1, arXiv:2310.07765#R3, arXiv:2611.06582#R5, arXiv:2611.06582#R7). counts: versions.V4.coverage_by_operation.training has no dataset-level breakdown that would establish SVHN coverage.

untested.what: An initialization-only trainable-depth sweep in language models, including explicitly identified billion-parameter models; parameter-bucket-resolved reproduction remains unestablished.
untested.basis: The transformer untested-parts lines leave maximum-depth comparisons open. arXiv:2302.10322 varies initialization within E-SPA, and arXiv:2605.25880#R1–R4 use a fixed-depth 194M model with recipe changes. counts: versions.V4.studies_by_size and versions.V4.coverage_by_operation.training.by_size contain only 'not stated'. This is missing scale annotation, not proof that every particular parameter scale is empirically absent.

wording_issues.phrase: Initialization decides training speed and trainable depth
wording_issues.issue: Initialization's effects depend on width, target geometry, learning-rate and training recipes. Finite-width first-layer controls and transformer ablations also limit attribution to signal preservation or initialization alone.

wording_issues.phrase: keep signals and gradients from vanishing or exploding across layers
wording_issues.issue: Preserving expected squared norms, forward variance or an infinite-width criticality condition is weaker than preserving typical useful signals and gradients in finite networks. The propagation statistic and width/depth regime need specifying.

The evidence mixes time to an accuracy threshold, early training accuracy, endpoint test accuracy and endpoint fitting quality. These support distinct learning outcomes; they do not all measure time to matched low training loss. For five-layer sinusoidal MLPs fitting Kodak images, training PSNR after 150 full-batch iterations is 0.46 ± 0.10 with Xavier uniform, 24.58 ± 0.05 with standard SIREN initialization and 42.83 ± 0.35 with weight scaling; uncertainties are standard deviations over five seeds. This row measures fixed-budget fitting quality with reported initialization controls.

wording_issues.phrase: orthogonal weights learn faster than Gaussian weights of the same variance
wording_issues.issue: The advantage requires suitable variance and optimization conditions. The original reports a negligible tanh advantage at weight variance 2; its cited comparisons use 10^5 training steps and batch size 10^3. Wide, small-learning-rate comparisons can be nearly identical in the NTK regime, while suitable deep tanh experiments outside that regime retain the advantage. Width-30, hidden-depth-30 tanh networks can fail with either initialization at noncritical CW=0.1 or 10. The shallow null comparison is outside the statement's very-deep condition and supplies no qualification here.

The 10,000-layer result uses specially tuned critical Delta-Orthogonal initialization and explicitly reports successful training and depth-independent learning time on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Exact training-accuracy endpoints are not stated; this does not make qualitative trainability indeterminate. The separate spatially uniform orthogonal experiment does not establish the result for arbitrary orthogonal kernels.
Some extensions use BN, WN, UNet skip connections or orthogonalization maintained during training. Their results do not isolate initial weight choice in an unnormalized plain network.

wording_issues.phrase: initializations matched to the activation function
wording_issues.issue: Successful recipes can additionally require sparse-connectivity corrections, graph topology, nonnegative-weight and bias constraints, or joint changes to activation parameters and input scaling. Activation matching alone does not describe these interventions. In the seven-hidden-layer MNIST ICNN experiment, randomized biases accompany jointly adjusted weight variance. The experiment sets β=1/2, with bias variance σb²=β(1−ρ*)σ*²; at ρ*=1/2 and σ*²=1, σb²=1/4. β itself is not the bias variance, despite the inconsistent Figure 7 caption. The explicitly reported training benefit concerns this MNIST setting, rather than the broader dataset/depth grid.

Several comparisons establish useful predictive performance at tested depths after a finite budget. They do not directly identify a maximum trainable depth or establish matched convergence times or training errors. In CIFAR-10 SGD experiments at L=300, EOC test accuracy is 30.25 ± 3.23% for FFNN-ReLU, 58.25 ± 0.43% for FFNN-Tanh and 76.25 ± 0.21% for CNN-ReLU, each against an approximately 10% Ordered baseline. These establish initialization-dependent learning at the tested depth. The source gives conflicting budgets: Section 5.2 states 150 epochs, while Table 2's caption states 160.

method_sensitivity.factor: Width relative to depth and finite-width correction
method_sensitivity.what: He initialization permits faster startup when width grows with depth, while fixed-width networks slow with increasing depth. Deep linear orthogonal initialization has an approximately depth-independent successful width threshold. Finite-width tanh correction raises the median squared-gradient ratio across 96 layers from 0.076 to 0.81. LeakyReLU Lyapunov corrections improve narrow-network outcomes over standard He and orthogonal scaling.

method_sensitivity.factor: Tanh variance, saturation, learning rate and depth
method_sensitivity.what: The original orthogonal advantage is negligible at tanh weight variance 2, with training duration 10^5 steps and batch size 10^3. Later comparisons find larger advantages at greater depth and larger learning rates. In arXiv:2004.05867, the advantage disappears in the NTK regime while suitable deep tanh experiments outside that regime retain it. Criticality does not eliminate saturation-related accuracy loss. In width-30 networks, off-critical CW=0.1 produces vanishing-gradient failure and CW=10 frequently diverges.

method_sensitivity.factor: Dropout, quantization and propagation depth scales
method_sensitivity.what: In depth-200 ReLU autoencoders with dropout retention p=0.6, dropout-aware initialization permits initial loss reduction where He initialization fails. Critical initialization uses σw²=2/μ₂=2p and σb=0; per-weight variance divides σw² by preceding-layer width. He forward variance overflows; critical forward variance stays roughly constant. In critically initialized MNIST/CIFAR-10 identity autoencoders, training and validation performance worsen with increasing depth and noise, and input-correlation information degrades. Constant-width theory predicts vanishing gradients, so forward-only preservation does not test V4's joint preservation condition. Dropout trainability boundaries depend on propagation depth scales; the cited Figure 7 experiments do not independently specify width. Quantized and binary-surrogate experiments relate trainable depth to propagation scales. The binary-surrogate 16,000-step panels report test accuracy; the authors describe depths beyond approximately 6ξ as untrainable at that budget.

method_sensitivity.factor: Cross-layer structure, mean alignment and representation rank
method_sensitivity.what: Shared orthogonal structure outperforms independent orthogonal initialization in deep narrow ReLU networks. Mean-alignment ablations retain useful performance without semi-orthogonality. Rank-increasing preparation improves subsequent depth-32 Fashion-MNIST optimization. In ReLU CNNs, the proposed representation-orthogonalizing initialization slows SGD relative to Xavier with 20 convolutions but outperforms Xavier with 80 convolutions. Both comparisons use SGD step size 0.001 and batch size 30, reporting means and 95% confidence intervals over 4 independent runs; numerical losses are not stated.

method_sensitivity.factor: Sample statistics, bias centering and normalization parameters
method_sensitivity.what: Adding per-feature bias centering to scale initialization accelerates ALL-CNN-C loss reduction under SGD and Adam with separately selected learning rates. Initial BN gamma or beta changes maximum trainable depth in the verdict-described MNIST experiments. Maintained ONI needs activation-aware √2 scaling for its deeper ReLU network, while its shallow counterpart shows no significant scaling benefit.

method_sensitivity.factor: Initialization balance, target geometry, relative updates and kernel shaping
method_sensitivity.what: Near-zero versus near-identity initialization changes linear-regression startup. In arXiv:1802.06509, near-identity initialization uses independent Gaussian entries with mean 0 and standard deviation 0.01, then adds 1 to each diagonal entry, including in rectangular matrices. Balanced initialization broadens the useful scale range, but the separate exact-identity initialization in arXiv:1810.02281 fails for the stated even-depth negative-eigenvalue target. In separate Fashion-MNIST controls, matching the first layer removes the remaining Crinit advantage over tuned gain within uncertainty; those controls lack retained rows. For ImageNet vanilla ReLU-family networks (50, 101 and 200 layers; K-FAC; 90 epochs), activation-matched TAT and EOC use hyperparameters selected by highest final validation accuracy. Authors report competitive or better EOC training accuracy and attribute TAT's gains to generalization; depth-specific differences are unreadable. This is contextual coverage, not a demonstrated failure of V4's initialization benefit.

method_sensitivity.factor: Optimizer, training interval and comparator protocol
method_sensitivity.what: ACI's relative performance changes with task, SGD versus Adam and training stage; the cited SGD experiments use 10^5 training examples and a 10^4-epoch limit. Looks-linear batch-ReLU comparisons use batch size 1,000 for proposed initialization versus 50,000 for Gaussian controls. Their endpoint errors support V4 trainability, without establishing V6 training speed; other comparisons vary shared versus layer-wise step sizes. IDInit's fixed-depth AllConv advantage is reported without warm-up. Fractional-moment CIFAR-10 comparisons use two convolutional layers, 20 fully connected layers and hidden width 64 over the first 50 epochs. ReLU and Leaky ReLU show initialization-dependent early training; linear activation shows little separation. The cited R5 and R8 values belong to linear activation, not Leaky ReLU.

method_sensitivity.factor: Sparse connectivity, density distribution and graph topology
method_sensitivity.what: Masked dense and sparsity-aware initializations produce different early gradient flow. Exact orthogonal initialization gives weaker training-dynamics improvements with SNIP/Synflow density distributions. Topology-aware GCN initialization restores gradients relative to default Glorot. ReLU GNN output scaling changes early training, with residual aggregation used to mitigate oversmoothing.

method_sensitivity.factor: Activation parameters, input scaling and stability neighborhood
method_sensitivity.what: Sparsifying-activation trainability depends on family, clipping, sparsity and variance-map slope. At sparsity 0.85, CReLU DNN test accuracy is 0.28±0.37 with m=1.74 and slope 0.9. CReLU CNNs remain near the ReLU baseline at sparsity 0.70; at sparsity 0.85 and slope 0.9, test accuracies are 0.66 for CReLU (m=1.74) and 0.29 for CST (m=1.53), versus baseline 0.70. At 90% target sparsity, 30-layer CReLU and CST DNNs train successfully at slope 0.7 with m=1.06 and 0.93 respectively; CST fails at slope 0.9, m=1.44. MRePU R12 shows observed trainability despite unstable evaluation. Increasing q* accelerates CReLU training-loss convergence while activation parameters and input scaling change jointly. Joint bias randomization and weight-variance adjustment enable seven-hidden-layer MNIST ICNN training; β=1/2 gives bias variance 1/4.

method_sensitivity.factor: Recurrent task, weight tying and transformer training recipe
method_sensitivity.what: Propagation-timescale predictions agree quantitatively with untied RNN experiments and qualitatively with tied-weight experiments. These MNIST experiments present the entire flattened image first, followed by Gaussian inputs, with T from 10 to 1000 and training for 10^3 optimization steps, approximately 10 epochs. Normal, chain and feedback-chain initializers differ on long-memory tasks. E-SPA shows little training-loss sensitivity among small query/key scales that all approximately preserve the intended attention initialization; this comparison cannot determine V4's benefit. Larger scales degrade performance. Residual-free transformer outcomes change with AdamW versus KL Shampoo and QK normalization versus depth-aware temperature scaling.
